b: MOA : Inhibit DNA gyrase (Gram-ve) + topoisomerase IV (Gram+ve) → bactericidal , concentration-dependent.
Ciprofloxacin = Gram-negatives/Pseudomonas; Levofloxacin = respiratory; Moxifloxacin = NO urinary excretion.
Side effects : tendinopathy/rupture (↑ with steroids), QT prolongation , seizures, peripheral neuropathy, avoid in children/pregnancy.
Resistance : GyrA mutations , efflux pumps, qnr genes (plasmid-mediated).
Mechanism: inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV → prevent DNA supercoiling/relaxation → DNA strand breaks → inability to replicate/repair DNA → bactericidal
Concentration-dependent killing — maximise Cmax; once or twice daily dosing
Excellent oral bioavailability (near-complete absorption — oral = IV for most indications)
Contraindicated in: children · pregnancy · myasthenia gravis (worsen neuromuscular blockade)

Several large-scale studies indicate that prophylaxis with a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) decreases morbidity and mortality rates among afebrile patients who are anticipated to have neutropenia of long duration.
Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone — Pseudomonas exacerbations — Tendon injury, QT prolongation
Management: Requires longer, more complex regimens with second-line drugs (e.g., fluoroquinolones, injectables like amikacin/kanamycin, bedaquiline, delamanid).

Underlying cause correction: Treat severe malaria, manage sepsis, correct hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia, discontinue QT-prolonging medicines (e.g., macrolides, fluoroquinolones, haloperidol), and treat underlying TB pericarditis or ischaemia.
Alternatives: Other options include fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin) or azithromycin.
Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin): QT-interval prolongation, dysglycaemia, tendon rupture.
Uncomplicated cystitis in non‑pregnant adult: Fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) — Fluoroquinolone PO — Excellent urinary penetration, low resistance in most Kenyan isolates.

qs.q: What is the primary enzymatic target of fluoroquinolones when acting against Gram-negative bacterial pathogens?
qs.e: Fluoroquinolones primarily target DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) in Gram-negative bacteria and topoisomerase IV in Gram-positives. Dihydropteroate synthase is inhibited by sulfonamides rather than quinolones.

qs.q: Which fluoroquinolone possesses excellent activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and is considered the best antipseudomonal quinolone in its class?
qs.e: Ciprofloxacin is the most potent quinolone against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Moxifloxacin undergoes hepatic elimination and is not used for urinary tract infections or Pseudomonas.

qs.q: Which side effect represents a prominent black-box warning associated with systemic fluoroquinolone therapy, especially in elderly patients taking corticosteroids?
qs.e: Fluoroquinolones carry a well-known risk of tendinopathy and Achilles tendon rupture, exacerbated by advanced age and corticosteroids. Aplastic anaemia is classically linked to chloramphenicol toxicity.

qs.q: What type of drug resistance is characterized by resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one second-line injectable drug, alongside MDR-TB?
qs.e: Extensive drug resistance requires resistance to a fluoroquinolone and a second-line injectable drug, in addition to multidrug resistance. Polydrug resistance involves multiple first-line drugs other than the mandatory Isoniazid and Rifampicin combination.

qs.q: Moxifloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that has activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis, including some multidrug-resistant strains. It is often used in combination with other antitubercular agents.
qs.e: While isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide are primary antitubercular drugs, moxifloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) is an important agent in treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) due to its activity against M. tuberculosis, including some strains resistant to first-line drugs.
